title: Disassemble, Assess and Reassemble Tractor Hydraulic Systems

lessons.title: Testing and dismantling hydraulic components
lessons.html:
Test before you strip

Hydraulic components are expensive and precise. Before dismantling, test the system to find which component is at fault. Use the workshop manual's test procedure, a flow meter and pressure gauges rated above system pressure, and the diagnostic tool for electronically controlled valves.

Typical tests

  • Pump flow test: flow at rated engine speed against a load set by the flow meter's restrictor. Low flow under load indicates pump wear.
  • Relief valve setting: pressure at which the relief valve opens.
  • Standby and load-sense pressure on closed-centre systems.
  • Cylinder drift test: how far a loaded cylinder drops over a set time, to separate cylinder seal leaks from valve leaks.
  • Oil temperature and condition: tests must be done at the specified oil temperature.

Safe preparation

  1. Lower implements and loaders, stop the engine and release pressure by cycling controls. Discharge accumulators as the manual shows.
  2. Clean the outside of components thoroughly before opening anything.
  3. Drain oil into clean containers and inspect it; keep a sample if needed.
  4. Cap and plug every opening immediately.

Dismantling components

  • Cylinders: secure in a vice or bench fixture, remove the gland with the correct spanner, withdraw the rod and piston slowly. Do not use compressed air to blow the piston out.
  • Valves: spools are matched to their bores; keep each spool with its own section and note orientation. Springs and detents must go back in the same place.
  • Pumps: mark housing sections for alignment before separating; note shim and port plate positions.

Work on a clean bench with lint-free cloths. A single grain of sand can jam a spool.

lessons.title: Assessing, rebuilding and commissioning hydraulics
lessons.html:
Assessment

ComponentChecks
Cylinder barrelScoring, bore wear, dents, straightness
Cylinder rodChrome damage, pitting, straightness
Seals and wipersCuts, hardening, extrusion
Gear pumpsWear tracks on housing, side plate wear, gear tooth damage
Piston pumpsPiston and bore wear, swash plate and valve plate scoring
Valve spools and boresScoring, sticking, spring condition
Hoses and fittingsAge, cracking, damaged threads, correct pressure rating

Measure against specifications in the workshop manual. Identify the root cause: scored parts mean contamination, burnt seals mean overheating, extruded seals mean excessive pressure or worn clearances. If contamination caused the failure, the whole system must be flushed or the new parts will fail too.

Rebuilding

  1. Use the correct seal kit for the component's part number.
  2. Lubricate seals with clean hydraulic oil. Use seal installation tools; never use screwdrivers that can cut seals.
  3. Check that seals face the correct direction.
  4. Torque piston nuts and gland nuts to specification and fit locking devices.
  5. Assemble valve sections with spools in their original bores.
  6. Fill pumps with clean oil before installing so they do not run dry on start-up.

Flushing and commissioning

  • Change all filters and, where contamination occurred, flush lines and the reservoir as the manual describes.
  • Fill with the specified oil through a filter.
  • Start at low idle, operate each function slowly to bleed air, and check the level.
  • Repeat the pressure and flow tests and compare with specification and with the results before repair.
  • Calibrate electronic hitch and valve settings with the diagnostic tool if required.
  • Check for leaks with cardboard, not hands.

Key points

  • Test flow, pressure and drift to find the faulty component before stripping.
  • Release pressure and discharge accumulators before opening any line.
  • Keep valve spools with their own bores and work in clean conditions.
  • Find the root cause and flush the system after contamination failures.
  • Retest pressures and flows after the rebuild.
